newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal seen reaching 3 pct deficit goal in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Portugal seen reaching 3 pct deficit goal in 1997.

text.p: Portugal should manage to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 in order to meet a target for joining the European single currency without having to resort to draconian measures recommended by the IMF, analysts said.
They said the strengthening of economic growth, improved tax collection procedures and moderate 1997 public sector wage increases should make it possible to achieve this goal.

"If the economy grows at rates above 2.5 percent and if there is greater efficiency in the tax system and moderate public sector wage increases, it will be possible to meet the three percent budget deficit target next year," said Isabel Cabral, economist with Lisbon broker Fincor.
A confidential IMF report published in Diario Economico newspaper recommended that Portugal should take tough action on state spending to ensure it meets the deficit target.
It suggested a freeze in public sector pay and cuts in civil servant jobs.
An alternative would be to raise taxes, it said. It recommended a rise in Value Added Tax (VAT) as the levels currently applied in Portugal were below European averages.

Antonio Pina Moura, secretary of state in the prime minister's office, disagreed with the recommendation and said Portugal would not have to cut jobs in order to reach the deficit target, a condition for joining the single currency.
Jose Luiz Alzola, analyst with Salomon Brothers in London, said he believed Portugal could hit the three percent target.
"It is possible," he said. "The government will have to make further adjustments to spending and taxation, but not much."
The Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres has said it expected to cut the budget deficit to four percent of GDP this year from around five percent in 1995.
It plans to cut the deficit to 2.9 percent in 1997.
Most analysts said they believed that public sector layoffs and significant tax increases were unlikely.
Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco told parliament last week the government would not raise taxes in 1997 for the second straight year.
"It is a little hasty of the IMF to talk of layoffs in the public sector or tax rises," said Fincor's Cabral.
Alzola said that prospects to bring down the budget deficit to three percent would benefit from moderate public sector wages growth and an easing of interest rates.
Analysts expect a further easing of key rates, which would reduce the burden of public sector debt service payments, boosting prospects for meeting the three percent target.
"I think that we should manage to beat the 4.2 percent deficit target for this year, which will give us a good starting point for 1997," Alzola said.
"Let's hope that economic growth speeds up to 2.5 percent in 1997, which will boost tax revenues," he added.
"But this is not enough. It is important that civil servants' salaries grow moderately, for example, between two and 2.5 percent, which should be close to the inflation forecasts."
Some analysts forecast economic growth of between 2.0 and 2.3 percent in 1996. The government has forecast growth at 2.7 percent this year.
-- Sergio Goncalves, Lisbon newsroom +351-1-3538254
